text: Writing a separate hand-coded test for every boundary value — zero, the threshold, max uint256 — is tedious and you'll still miss cases. Fuzz testing solves this differently: give the test function a parameter instead of a hard-coded value, and Forge calls it repeatedly with randomly generated inputs, 256 times by default.

Any function parameter Forge recognizes — uint, int, address, bytes — gets fuzzed automatically; you don't opt in per parameter. You just write the assertion once, and Forge supplies the inputs, not you.

Most functions don't accept any uint256 — they have real constraints, like an amount that can't exceed a balance. Two cheatcodes narrow the input space. vm.assume rejects any run outside a condition — too many rejections and Forge gives up. bound() clamps the fuzzed value into a range instead, so every run counts, which is usually the better choice.

foundry.toml's fuzz table controls the campaign: runs sets how many random inputs Forge generates per test, max_test_rejects caps how many vm.assume rejections it tolerates, and a fixed seed makes a fuzzing run reproducible — which matters when a failure needs to be debugged by re-running the exact same sequence.

A fuzz test still only calls one function, once, per run — it doesn't test sequences of calls across multiple functions and actors. That's exactly what Lesson 3's invariant testing adds. You're ready for Lesson 3 once you can explain why bound() is usually preferred over vm.assume.
